subject: biology
title: The Human Nervous System
welcome_lead: Today's adventure: The Human Nervous System — AQA GCSE Biology (8461) specification, section 4.5.2.
meta_desc: GCSE Biology (AQA) practice covering The Human Nervous System, specification section 4.5.2.
final_note: You worked through The Human Nervous System — 24 specification statements.

concepts.def: The system of receptors, neurones and the central nervous system that enables humans to react to their surroundings and to coordinate their behaviour.
A cell or structure that detects a stimulus, for example the light receptors in the retina or the temperature receptors in the skin.
A nerve cell that carries information as electrical impulses from receptors to the central nervous system, and from the central nervous system to effectors.
The brain and spinal cord. The CNS coordinates the response of effectors to the information it receives from receptors.
A structure that brings about the response. Effectors may be muscles contracting or glands secreting hormones.
The sequence stimulus → receptor → coordinator → effector → response, which describes how the body detects and responds to a change.
An automatic and rapid response to a stimulus that does not involve the conscious part of the brain.
The pathway taken by an impulse in a reflex action: receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone in the CNS → motor neurone → effector.
The junction between two neurones. A chemical is released and diffuses across the gap, setting off a new electrical impulse in the next neurone.
The organ that controls complex behaviour. It is made of billions of interconnected neurones and has different regions that carry out different functions.
The outer, folded region of the brain, responsible for consciousness, intelligence, memory and language.
The region at the back and base of the brain, responsible for coordinating muscular activity and balance.
The region of the brain stem that controls unconscious activities such as heart rate and breathing rate.
The sclera is the tough white outer layer that protects the eye; the cornea is the transparent front part of that layer, which refracts light entering the eye.
The coloured ring of muscle that controls the size of the pupil, and so controls how much light enters the eye.
The retina is the light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye, containing receptors sensitive to light intensity and colour; the optic nerve carries impulses from the retina to the brain.
A ring of muscle and the ligaments that attach it to the lens. Together they change the shape of the lens during accommodation.
The process of changing the shape of the lens to focus on near or distant objects.
A defect of the eye in which rays of light from a distant object focus in front of the retina. It is generally treated with a concave spectacle lens that makes the rays focus on the retina.
A defect of the eye in which rays of light focus behind the retina. It is generally treated with a convex spectacle lens that refracts the rays so that they focus on the retina.

Spectacle lenses refract light rays so that they focus on the retina. New technologies include hard and soft contact lenses, laser surgery to change the shape of the cornea, and a replacement lens in the eye.

The centre in the brain that monitors and controls body temperature. It contains receptors sensitive to the temperature of the blood and receives nervous impulses from temperature receptors in the skin.
The widening of blood vessels supplying the skin when body temperature is too high, which, with sweat produced from the sweat glands, causes a transfer of energy from the skin to the environment.
The narrowing of blood vessels supplying the skin when body temperature is too low, which reduces the transfer of energy from the skin to the environment.

mcqs.q: A single neurone carries impulses from a receptor in the toe to the spinal cord. Which statement best explains how this structure is adapted to its function?
options: It is long, so impulses reach the CNS quickly.
It detects the stimulus and causes the response.
It is part of the central nervous system.
It carries the impulse without using the CNS.
mcqs.explain: Information from receptors passes along cells (neurones) as electrical impulses to the central nervous system, so one long cell carries the impulse the whole way to the spinal cord without delay.

mcqs.q: Effectors in the human body may be:
options: muscles contracting or glands secreting
receptors detecting light and sound levels
skeletal muscles moving bones at a joint
neurones carrying impulses into the brain
mcqs.explain: The CNS coordinates the response of effectors, which may be muscles contracting or glands secreting hormones.

mcqs.q: In a reflex arc, what is the function of the relay neurone?
options: It carries the impulse to the conscious brain.
It links the sensory neurone to the motor neurone.
It carries the electrical impulse across the synapse.
It carries the impulse from the skin without the CNS.
mcqs.explain: In a reflex arc the sensory neurone passes the impulse across a synapse to a relay neurone in the CNS, which passes it on to the motor neurone that carries the impulse to the effector.

mcqs.q: Why is a reflex action important when a person touches a very hot object?
options: It gives the person time to decide how to act.
It keeps the impulse out of the nervous system.
It is automatic and rapid, so injury is reduced.
It lets the receptor make the response itself.
mcqs.explain: Reflex actions are automatic and rapid; the hand is moved away from the stimulus before the conscious part of the brain is involved, which limits the damage done.

mcqs.q: A table shows one student's mean reaction time in three trials: trial 1, 0.28 s; trial 2, 0.24 s; trial 3, 0.21 s. What do these data show?
options: The reaction time fell across the trials.
The reaction time rose across the trials.
The student reacted more slowly each time.
The results apply to other students too.
mcqs.explain: Reading the values in order from the table shows a decrease from 0.28 s to 0.21 s, which is the pattern the data support.

mcqs.q: Four students have mean reaction times of 0.15 s, 0.22 s, 0.28 s and 0.31 s. These values are drawn as a bar chart. Which statement about the chart is correct?
options: The tallest bar is the fastest time.
The shortest bar is the slowest time.
The tallest bar is the 0.31 s time.
Each bar stands for the whole group.
mcqs.explain: Translating the numbers into graphical form, bar height is proportional to reaction time, so the largest value, 0.31 s, gives the tallest bar.

mcqs.q: A patient can no longer coordinate their movements or keep their balance after an injury to the brain. Which is the most likely cause?
options: Damage within the medulla
The cerebellum is damaged
Cerebral cortex is damaged
Damage to the spinal cord
mcqs.explain: The cerebellum is the region of the brain responsible for coordinating muscular activity and balance, which are the functions the patient has lost.

mcqs.q: Neuroscientists want to find out which region of a patient's brain controls speech. Which statement explains why this is difficult?
options: Damaged brain regions are simple to repair.
MRI scanning shows which cells are working.
Each region of the brain does the same job.
The brain is complex and easily damaged.
mcqs.explain: The brain is made of billions of interconnected neurones, and its complexity and delicacy make investigating brain function and treating brain damage and disease very difficult.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly relates a structure of the eye to its function?
options: The cornea changes shape to focus images.
The iris narrows the pupil in dim lighting.
The ciliary muscles relax for near objects.
The retina contains receptors for light.
mcqs.explain: The eye is a sense organ containing receptors sensitive to light intensity and colour, and these receptors are found in the retina at the back of the eye.

mcqs.q: A person walks out of bright sunlight into a dark room. What happens in the eye?
options: The iris muscles make the pupil narrower.
The ciliary muscles make the lens thicker.
The cornea changes shape to admit light.
The iris muscles make the pupil wider.
mcqs.explain: The eye adapts to dim light by the iris muscles widening the pupil, so more light enters the eye and reaches the receptors in the retina.

mcqs.q: A student looks up from a book and focuses on a tree in the distance. What happens in the eye?
options: The ciliary muscles contract and the lens thickens.
The suspensory ligaments loosen and the lens bulges.
The cornea changes shape and the lens stays thin.
The ciliary muscles relax and the lens is pulled thin.
mcqs.explain: To focus on a distant object the ciliary muscles relax, the suspensory ligaments are pulled tight and the lens is pulled thin, so it only slightly refracts the light rays.

mcqs.q: A ray diagram shows light from a distant object coming to a focus in front of the retina. Which defect is shown, and how is it corrected?
options: Myopia, corrected with a convex lens.
Hyperopia, corrected with a convex lens.
Myopia, corrected with a concave lens.
Hyperopia, corrected with a concave lens.
mcqs.explain: Rays focusing in front of the retina show myopia (short sightedness); a concave spectacle lens spreads the rays out so that they do focus on the retina.

mcqs.q: A person is exercising hard and their body temperature rises above normal. What happens in the skin?
options: Blood vessels dilate and sweat is produced.
Blood vessels move nearer the skin surface.
Blood vessels constrict and shivering starts.
The skin cools the body without the brain.
mcqs.explain: If the body temperature is too high, blood vessels dilate (vasodilation) and sweat is produced from the sweat glands; both mechanisms cause a transfer of energy from the skin to the environment.

mcqs.q: A person waits at a bus stop in cold weather and their body temperature begins to fall. How does the body raise it again?
options: Blood vessels dilate and shivering begins.
Blood vessels constrict and shivering starts.
Narrowing blood vessels cause the shivering.
The skin warms the blood without using the brain.
mcqs.explain: If the body temperature is too low, blood vessels constrict (vasoconstriction) and sweating stops, reducing energy transfer from the skin, while skeletal muscles contract (shiver), releasing energy that warms the body.
